clue.text: One to berate kilts drunkenly about start of Hogmanay?

indicators.note: the shuffled letters go around the next piece
staggering drunkenly, the letters of the two words lurch into a new order
only the opening letter of the Scottish New Year word is taken

explanation.surface: A tipsy Scot at New Year rails against kilts, talking nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: Indicators: 'drunkenly' (anagram), 'about' (container), 'start of' (first letter). Hogmanay is the Scottish New Year's Eve celebration; the question mark flags that such a ranting reveller is only an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A blatherskite is a person who talks at length without sense, so it is one who blathers, defined here simply as a person.

clue.text: Assassin to kick hard

parts.note: to kick something is to boot it
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: An instruction to a killer to lash out with a heavy kick.
explanation.walkthrough: John Wilkes Booth shot Abraham Lincoln in 1865.
explanation.definitionFit: John Wilkes Booth was the actor who killed President Lincoln, the archetypal American political killer.

clue.text: Mistakes made by bear perhaps over "the bare necessities"

indicators.note: in a down entry one piece sits over the other, so it comes first
perhaps signals that the four letters may be arranged some other way

parts.note: rations are the basic allowance of food, the bare necessities of life

explanation.surface: Baloo the bear of The Jungle Book, singing The Bare Necessities, makes some blunders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges BEAR into ABER, and 'over' puts it above RATIONS in this down entry. The surface nods to Baloo's song from the Disney Jungle Book, in a Kipling-themed puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Aberrations are deviations from what is right or normal, hence errors or slips.

clue.text: Mr Creakle to rage about his mortar board, say

parts.note: Mr Creakle is the brutal headmaster of Salem House in Dickens's David Copperfield

indicators.note: about here means the letters of the following word are turned around into a new order

explanation.surface: A Dickensian schoolmaster flies into a fury over his academic cap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges RAGE into GEAR. A mortar board is the square academic cap a headmaster wears, so 'say' marks it as an example; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A mortarboard is a flat square cap, one example of the hats and helmets worn on the head.

clue.text: Movie — one following Rudyard's first poem and another movie

indicators.note: following places the single letter after the pieces before it
the first letter of the novelist's forename is the one taken

parts.note: If is Kipling's famous poem of advice to his son
If.... is Lindsay Anderson's 1968 film about a rebellion at a boarding school
one as the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A film is listed after Kipling's best-known poem and a second picture.
explanation.walkthrough: Rififi is Jules Dassin's 1955 French heist film. Take R, from 'first' of Rudyard, then IF the poem, IF the film, and I placed last by 'following'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rififi is a classic French crime film famous for its silent half-hour safe-cracking scene.

clue.text: Book about chap lacking energy

indicators.note: about turns the shortened name round to read backwards
lacking means the energy symbol is taken away from the name

parts.note: Mike is a common man's name, so any chap
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A book about a listless fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacking' drops E from MIKE to leave MIK, and 'about' turns it backwards. 'Book' looks like a verb or a general noun, but it is Kipling's 1901 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Kim is Kipling's novel of an Irish orphan boy caught up in the Great Game in British India.

clue.text: Bears surrounding the nameless Hydra's lair. Bears!

indicators.note: surrounding means the first piece is wrapped round the second

parts.note: to tote something is to carry or bear it

indicators.note: nameless removes N, the abbreviation for name

parts.note: Lerna was the swamp where Heracles fought the many-headed Hydra

explanation.surface: A warning about creatures carrying things around the monster's swamp, ending in a cry of alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: Indicators: 'nameless' drops N, the name abbreviation, and 'surrounding' wraps the result. The two 'Bears' are different senses: carries in the wordplay, puts up with in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear something unpleasant is to put up with it, to endure or accept it.

clue.text: Mostly calm swim in Sri Lanka

indicators.note: mostly signals that the word loses its last letter

parts.note: calm means serene
a dip is a short swim

explanation.surface: A quiet bathe off the coast of an island in the Indian Ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mostly' cuts SERENE to SEREN. Serendip, the old Persian name for the island, gave Horace Walpole the word serendipity.
explanation.definitionFit: Serendip is an archaic name for the island now called Sri Lanka, formerly Ceylon.

clue.text: Tennis player featured in the first half of a Maugham collection

indicators.note: only the front four of the eight letters are kept, the rest cut away

parts.note: Ashenden is Somerset Maugham's collection of linked spy stories

explanation.surface: A tennis star appears in the opening pages of a short-story book by Maugham.
explanation.walkthrough: Ashenden, or The British Agent (1928), is drawn from Maugham's own wartime spying. Keeping 'the first half of' its eight letters leaves four.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Ashe won the US Open, the Australian Open and Wimbledon, the first Black man to take the men's title there.

clue.text: Rhetorical question, flipping answer found to Kierkegaard's coinage

indicators.note: flipping turns the whole run of pieces over so it reads backwards

parts.note: found here means met, as in came upon
the ore is a small Danish coin, the currency of Kierkegaard's Denmark

explanation.surface: A question is turned round when its answer is sought in a coinage of the Danish philosopher.
explanation.walkthrough: One indicator, 'flipping', reverses A + MET + ORE (AMETORE) as a whole. 'Coinage' suggests a coined word, the philosopher's jargon, but it is a Danish coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Erotema is the rhetorician's term for a question asked for effect, not for an answer.

clue.text: Sorcerer's apprentice, endlessly hard worker, in thrall of timeless magician

indicators.note: being in thrall of someone means held within their power, so one piece sits inside the other
timeless removes T, the abbreviation for time

parts.note: Faust is the legendary scholar-magician who sold his soul to the Devil

indicators.note: endlessly removes the final letter of the animal

parts.note: a mule is proverbially a beast that works hard

explanation.surface: A wizard's assistant, a tireless drudge, is under the spell of an ageless magus.
explanation.walkthrough: Indicators: 'endlessly' and 'timeless' trim the two pieces, and 'in thrall of' holds one inside the other. In Goethe, Faust's attendant Wagner is called his famulus.
explanation.definitionFit: A famulus is an attendant or servant to a scholar or magician, especially in medieval tales.

clue.text: Disturbingly, Pinero has husband not at home in The Magistrate

indicators.note: disturbingly means the remaining letters are stirred up into a new order
not here means the following letters are removed from the dramatist's name

parts.note: in means at home

explanation.surface: In Pinero's farce The Magistrate, a husband is out of the house, with alarming results.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes IN from PINERO, leaving PERO; add H and 'Disturbingly' rearranges the lot. Pinero's farce The Magistrate (1885) makes the definition look like part of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The ephors were the five elected magistrates of ancient Sparta who oversaw even the kings.

clue.text: "The captain, (…) at the same time, put spurs to his very fine —" (Washington Irving)

definitions.text: "The captain, (…) at the same time, put spurs to his very fine —" (Washington Irving)

parts.words: "The captain, (…) at the same time, put spurs to his very fine —" (Washington Irving)
parts.note: a quotation with a blank to fill: the missing words are a mount received as a present, from the proverb about not inspecting its teeth

explanation.surface: A line from Washington Irving with its last words missing.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in clue: supply the words that end the quotation. The proverb 'never look a gift horse in the mouth' warns against finding fault with a present.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse given as a present is the subject of the proverb warning against examining a free offering's teeth.

clue.text: Domestic cricketer coming under TV doctor

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming under puts the second piece beneath the first

parts.note: Dr Gregory House is the misanthropic doctor in the American TV series House
the keeper is the wicketkeeper, the cricket fielder behind the stumps

explanation.surface: A home-grown cricketer comes on after a television medic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming under' places KEEPER below HOUSE in this down entry. 'Domestic' looks like an adjective (home-grown) but is the noun, a household servant.
explanation.definitionFit: A domestic is a household servant, and one who runs a household is the head servant of that kind.

clue.text: Corrupt, for the most part not a timid emperor

indicators.note: corrupt means the letters are spoiled into a different order
for the most part means the word loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A bold, depraved emperor, mostly unlike a shy one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for the most part' trims NOT to NO; 'Corrupt' rearranges NO + A + TIMID. Domitian (AD 81-96) was remembered as a cruel tyrant, which suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Domitian was a Roman ruler of the Flavian dynasty, son of Vespasian and brother of Titus.

clue.text: Cutting edge Spanish artist about the last thing in chic — that's how I see it!

indicators.note: about means the painter's name goes around the next letter

parts.note: Joan Miro was the Catalan surrealist painter

indicators.note: only the final letter of the fashionable word is used

parts.note: to me is the phrase for in my opinion, how I see things

explanation.surface: Fashion's latest word: a Spanish artist at the forefront of chic, in my view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts C, from 'the last thing in' chic, inside MIRO, then TO ME follows. 'Cutting edge' looks like the trendy phrase but is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A microtome is a laboratory instrument that slices specimens very thinly for viewing under a microscope.

clue.text: Tales with deserved appeal to those on the right

parts.note: deserved means just, as in a just reward
SOS is the distress signal, an appeal for help
the Tories are Britain's right-wing Conservative party

explanation.surface: Stories that call out to conservatives and get what they merit.
explanation.walkthrough: Tories, members of Britain's Conservative Party, are 'those on the right'.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's Just So Stories are a set of children's fables explaining how animals came to be as they are.

clue.text: With which The Doors of Perception entrances?

definitions.text: With which The Doors of Perception entrances?

parts.words: With which The Doors of Perception entrances?
parts.note: doors are gaps for passing through, and 'entrances' read as a noun names more such ways in; Huxley's book title begins the list

explanation.surface: Asking what Huxley's mescaline book uses to enthral its readers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entrances' looks like a verb, to enthral, but read as a noun it means ways in, like doors. The Doors of Perception is Aldous Huxley's 1954 essay on mescaline.
explanation.definitionFit: Doors and entrances are gaps through which one passes, so they are apertures of this kind.

clue.text: Girl is able, we hear, to meet prize-winning physicist

indicators.note: we hear means the words are judged by their sound, not their spelling

parts.note: a girl's name, Milly, followed by can, meaning is able

explanation.surface: A young woman manages, it is said, to be introduced to a Nobel laureate.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Millikan won the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physics for measuring the charge on the electron.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Millikan was an American experimental scientist who received the Nobel Prize in 1923.

clue.text: Title of one that's mischievous, having narrow-minded second accomplice

annotationWithheld.why: Title of one that's mischievous, having narrow-minded second accomplice (4,2,5,4) for PUCK OF POOK'S HILL: PUCK and SHILL (accomplice) are clear, but no reading of 'narrow-minded second' gives POOK or POO, so the wordplay cannot be shown honestly
annotationWithheld.clue: Title of one that's mischievous, having narrow-minded second accomplice

clue.text: One with possibly nice discernment missing the start of Terminator

indicators.note: possibly means the four letters may be arranged another way
missing means the following letter is dropped from the word for discernment

parts.note: taste is discernment in aesthetic matters

indicators.note: the start of means the opening letter of the film title is the one to drop

explanation.surface: A filmgoer of fine judgment skips the opening of a Schwarzenegger action film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges NICE into CINE; 'missing' drops T, 'the start of' Terminator, from TASTE to leave ASTE. 'One with' only introduces the film lover the clue describes.
explanation.definitionFit: A cineaste is a film enthusiast, a devotee of the cinema, here just a person.

clue.text: When a rest is right out perhaps? No way!

definitions.text: When a rest is right out perhaps? No way!

indicators.note: perhaps signals the remaining letters can be arranged another way
out means the letter for right is taken away from the phrase

explanation.surface: A rest taken when one is out of it, then a protest that it is not possible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' removes R from A REST IS, and 'perhaps' rearranges the remaining six letters. The whole clue is also the definition: an afternoon nap is when a rest takes over.
explanation.definitionFit: A siesta is a short sleep taken after lunch in hot countries, a time set aside for resting.

clue.text: See 19
What's opened on rising? This, in part

definitions.text: What's opened on rising? This, in part

indicators.note: on rising in a down entry means the run is read upwards, backwards
in part means only a portion of the words is taken, a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: Asking what someone opens when they get up in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: Inside 'What's opened' lies TSOP, which 'on rising' turns upwards in this down entry. The whole clue is also the definition: the morning mail is opened on getting up.
explanation.definitionFit: Letters delivered each morning are torn open at breakfast, the mail of daily routine.

clue.text: One of The Ambassadors, Anglo-Greek characters

parts.note: el is the English name for the letter L, an English character
chi is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A figure in Holbein's painting The Ambassadors is an English-Greek mix.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ambassadors is Holbein's double portrait in the National Gallery, so the definition looks like part of the surface. Elchi is an old word for an envoy from the Turkish court.
explanation.definitionFit: Elchi is a Turkish and Persian word for an envoy or emissary, used in English travel writing.

clue.text: Lee initially told off about his surname

indicators.note: about means the old verb form goes around the next letter

parts.note: chid is an old past tense of chide, to scold or tell off

indicators.note: initially means only the first letter of the name is used

explanation.surface: Lee was scolded over his family name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts L, from 'initially' Lee, inside CHID. Lee Child is the British author of the Jack Reacher thrillers, so 'his' points back to Lee.
explanation.definitionFit: Lee Child is the pen name of Jim Grant, writer of the Jack Reacher novels, so this is that author's last name.

clue.text: See 16
Seen to be sick twice when viewingKill Bill

indicators.note: the run is found by looking inside the film title, and the word sits there twice over

explanation.surface: Watching Tarantino's Kill Bill makes one feel queasy, twice over.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits in both words of the title Kill Bill, which is why the clue says 'twice'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill is the standard synonym for unwell or poorly.

clue.text: Writer about endless fish . fish ..

indicators.note: about turns the shortened fish round so it reads backwards
endless removes the last letter of the first fish

parts.note: a pike is a large freshwater fish
the ling is a long sea fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: An author's piece on a couple of fish.
explanation.walkthrough: Indicators: 'endless' trims the first fish and 'about' turns what is left backwards. The whole puzzle is themed on this author's work.
explanation.definitionFit: Rudyard Kipling was the author of The Jungle Book, Kim and the Just So Stories.

clue.text: Polite, so like Judith Martin?

definitions.meaning: Judith Martin writes the etiquette column Miss Manners, so she is full of manners

explanation.surface: Asking whether an etiquette columnist is courteous.
explanation.definitionFit: Polite people have good social graces, behaving properly in company.
